title: Binance halts withdrawals after record hack; digital assets, crypto stocks slump
full_text:
Investing.com - Binance suspended withdrawals on Friday after hackers stole $6.3 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange in the biggest heist in the history of the digital asset industry. Get more breaking news on Bitcoin and the crypto industry by subscribing to InvestingPro
In a statement, the exchange said it was working with partners to freeze about $3 billion in affected assets and stressed that "user funds were safe." Binance will also cover all losses from its funds.
Withdrawals will remain temporarily suspended until security checks are completed, Binance said. The company expects to resume withdrawals by Sunday.
The exchange said that the incident stemmed from a compromised development and operations engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to carry out unauthorized withdrawals. There was no evidence of any wallet private key leak.
Citing U.S. blockchain analysis groups TRM Labs and Chainalysis, Reuters reported that the majority of heist took place over 20 minutes starting late on Thursday, with the hackers appearing to have exploited Binance’s transaction authorization procedures. Both firms said they were confident that North Korea’s "elite hacking unit," known as TraderTraitor, was likely behind the cyberattack.
Glassnode data showed $1.66 billion in stablecoin USDT, $1.45 billion in Bitcoin, and $767 million in stablecoin USDC were drained from the exchange. Ether and several other smaller altcoins were also siphoned from the exchange.
Separately, USDC operator Circle said it had frozen over 800 million USDC associated with the hack, while stablecoin grouop Tether said it froze over 1.567 billion USDT associated with the hack.
Bitcoin fell following news of the hack, extending losses from earlier this week. The world’s largest token was last down by 3.2% to $77,484.1, after initially dropping to as low as $76,518. Ether fell 3.7% to $2,235.94.
Binance’s native BNB token pared initial losses to trade down 5.5%. Glassnode said the exchange’s balance of BNB was "left untouched."
Losses spilled over into crypto stocks, with U.S. exchange Coinbase (NASDAQ:COIN) and Bitcoin treasury Strategy (NASDAQ:MSTR) falling more than 5% in premarket trading Friday. Robinhood shares also tumbled 6.3%.
(Vahid Karaahmetovic and Scott Kanowsky contributed to this report.)

title: Intel plummets over 28% as weak forecast overshadows earnings beat
full_text:
Investing.com — Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) shares shed more than a fourth of their value in U.S. trading on Friday morning, after the chipmaker forecast fourth-quarter earnings and revenue well below Wall Street expectations.
Third-quarter adjusted earnings came in at $0.52 per share, beating analyst estimates of $0.40. Revenue rose 21% year over year to $16.5 billion, slightly above consensus of $16.48 billion.
The outlook was considerably weaker. Intel forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, below analyst expectations of $17.08 billion. At the midpoint, the range implies a shortfall of about 9%. Adjusted earnings are expected to reach $0.25 per share, compared with consensus of $0.44.
The guidance comes as Intel faces contrasting trends across its businesses, with strong demand for server CPUs helping offset weakness in the PC market.
“Despite near-term headwinds across the PC industry, demand for our CPUs remains robust,” Chief Executive Lip-Bu Tan said, adding that the results reflected improving execution, expanded supply and progress in process technology.
Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner said Intel expects PC market weakness to continue through at least the first half of next year.
Revenue from Intel’s Client Computing and Physical AI Group fell 5% year over year to $8.1 billion in the third quarter, reflecting the industry slowdown. By contrast, revenue from its Data Center and AI segment surged 78% to $7.3 billion, marking the strongest data-center revenue growth in 15 years, according to Zinsner.
Intel’s profitability outlook also disappointed. Adjusted gross margin expanded to 44.1% in the third quarter from 40% a year earlier, but the company expects the metric to decline to 38% in the fourth quarter.
"Client easy comps will not materialize until 2H27, while we continue to model share loss in both segments in 2027," Baird analysts said in a client note.
Intel Foundry revenue increased 58% year over year to $6.7 billion. The company generated $5.1 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter, while investors continue to assess whether its manufacturing business can attract enough external customers to support its long-term investment plans.
(Scott Kanowsky contributed reporting)

title: Amazon shares drop as holiday forecast misses Wall Street targets
full_text:
Investing.com -- Amazon missed quarterly financial estimates, while the e-commerce and tech giant’s negative free cash flow ballooned amid elevated spending on artificial intelligence.
Shares of the company were down more than 4% in early U.S. trading on Friday
The Seattle, Washington-based firm’s results come at a time when AI spending has been under intense scrutiny. Concerns have soared over the billions of dollars being poured into AI infrastructure, or the combined hardware and software stack needed to handle massive data and computing power used to build and train AI processes.
Worries have also increased about the huge amounts of debt being issued by companies to fund these AI infrastructure buildouts, which in turn has contributed to a sell-off in government debt in the U.S. and across the world.
Amazon said free cash flow was negative $42.4 billion for the trailing twelve months, driven primarily by a Y/Y increase of $94.8 billion in purchases of property and equipment, mainly reflecting investments in AI.
Amazon, through its market-leading cloud unit Amazon Web Services (AWS), has become a major AI player and a so-called hyperscaler, investing heavily in building and operating large-scale data centers. Other AI hyperscalers include Meta Platforms, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Oracle.
"We believe mgmt continues to earn the right to invest despite the negative NT FCF impact as these investments are becoming increasingly de-risked," analysts at Truist said, while adding that the AMZN stock remains "one of the best plays on the secular growth of AI/Cloud, eCom, and Ads, all at a compelling valuation."
The world’s fifth-largest publicly listed firm said AWS revenue was $45.98 billion in Q3 2026, a surge of 39.3% Y/Y and marking the fastest growth in nearly five years.
“Our AWS investment in functionality and infrastructure is working, with over 39% year-over-year revenue growth in Q3 ($184 billion revenue run rate) and projected revenue growth rates of over 40% both in 2027 and in 2028,” AMZN top boss Andy Jassy said in a statement.
Amazon has also gained a notable foothold in the AI industry through its multi-billion dollar investments in leading AI frontier lab Anthropic. The Claude-developer unveiled its initial public offering filing earlier this week, and is targeting what could become the biggest market debut in history.
Looking at Amazon’s overall results, it earned $1.89 per share on revenue of $201.94 billion for its Q3 2026. Analysts had expected a profit of $1.96 per share on revenue of $202.10 billion.
The bottom-line was hit by pre-tax gains of $9.5 billion in Q3 2025 that was included in non-operating income (expense) from Amazon’s investments in Anthropic. Meanwhile, the top-line saw a $900 million unfavorable impact from Y/Y changes in foreign exchange rates.
Turning to guidance for Q4, Amazon sees revenue of $240 billion to $247 billion. The consensus estimate had been for revenue of $244.30 billion. AMZN also kept its full-year 2026 capital expenditures forecast unchanged at about $220 billion.
(Anuron Mitra contributed to this report.)

title: Reddit shares plunge 23% on DAUs deceleration, weak guidance
full_text:
Investing.com -- Reddit reported third-quarter results that topped analyst estimates, but shares sank sharply after the social media company issued a weaker-than-expected revenue outlook and warned of accelerating declines in search referral traffic.
The stock is down about 22% shortly after the open on Friday.
Reddit reported adjusted earnings of $1.40 per share, beating the consensus estimate of $1.33. Revenue rose 53% year over year to $895 million, above expectations of $874.9 million.
However, the company forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $1.00 billion to $1.03 billion, putting the midpoint of $1.015 billion below Wall Street’s $1.05 billion estimate.
The outlook comes as Reddit faces mounting pressure from changes in how users discover content online. Search referral traffic declined meaningfully in the third quarter, with the downturn accelerating toward the end of the period, CEO Steve Huffman said in a shareholder letter.
In October, search traffic fell by more than 1 million referrals per week on average. If the trend continues, Reddit warned that daily active unique users (DAUs) could decline by a low-double-digit percentage in the fourth quarter from its current base of 130.3 million.
Reddit’s DAUs grew 12% in the third quarter, a 6 percentage point slowdown from the previous quarter. The shortfall came mainly from U.S. logged-out users as Google’s AI Overviews cut referral traffic from one of Reddit’s largest user acquisition channels.
"RDDT’s delivery of strong Revenue/EBITDA growth (53%/70%) was overshadowed by worsening U.S. DAU declines, as increased prevalence of AI Overview negatively impacted referral traffic," Jefferies analyst John Colantuoni said.
"Growth is also expected to slow in 4Q, which is likely to raise concern about sustainability. We think the stock could be rangebound near-term until a recovery in user trends emerges, but still like the long-term story as monetization upside helps drive peer-leading revenue growth," he added.
Weekly active uniques grew 16% to 515.2 million.
KeyBanc Capital Markets downgraded Reddit after the earnings release. “We are downgrading shares of RDDT from OW to SW as our thesis is not playing out; search traffic is a larger headwind than envisioned (potential for a LDD% q/q decline in 4Q), and this creates more uncertainty around ’27E/’28E revenue and EBITDA," they wrote.
Separately, Citizens also cut the stock to Market Perform from Outperform, citing the sequential deceleration in U.S. DAUs. "Reddit will begin testing a logged in user experience as it expects to receive increasingly less traffic from Google, which is a headwind for top-of-funnel and reengaging users."
Reddit CEO Huffman said the company was focusing on growing its logged-in and app audiences, which account for more than 80% of Reddit’s monetization. Reddit plans to improve user retention, expand app adoption and begin testing a primarily logged-in experience in select markets outside the U.S. in the fourth quarter.
"Our business is growing because the Reddit experience captures the human experience in a way that no other platform can replicate," Huffman said. He added that surpassing $3 billion in revenue over the past 12 months demonstrated the strength of Reddit as a destination and the differentiated value of its platform.
Advertising remained a key growth driver during the quarter, with revenue increasing 54% year over year to $847 million. Net income rose 74% to $283 million, equivalent to a 32% net margin, while adjusted EBITDA climbed 70% to $402 million, representing a 45% margin.
Reddit forecast fourth-quarter adjusted EBITDA of $480 million to $510 million. The company also repurchased approximately 670,000 shares for $100 million during the third quarter.
Vahid Karaahmetovic contributed to this report.

title: Oil hits six-month highs as Hormuz attacks threaten Iran peace efforts
full_text:
Investing.com -- Oil prices ended October at six-month highs as attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz intensified, complicating diplomatic efforts to end the U.S.-Israel war with Iran.
Brent crude futures settled Friday at $117.64 a barrel, up 2.4%, after touching $118. U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 2.1% to $104.12. Brent gained 13.6% in October and WTI climbed 15.2%.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said four oil tankers caught fire following incidents in or near Hormuz on Friday, including vessels it said struck naval mines after entering unauthorized routes. The claims could not be independently verified.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency separately reported a projectile striking a tanker leaving the strait and another vessel catching fire after a strike south of Iran’s Lavan Island. The latter crew was reported safe.
A tally of UKMTO reports showed at least 35 attacks on shipping in the Gulf and Hormuz during October, the highest monthly count since the conflict began in February.
Shipping traffic has improved but remains sharply depressed. UKMTO recorded 122 outbound and 155 inbound transits in the week through October 28, roughly 70% below pre-war levels.
President Donald Trump said Friday that talks with Iran were continuing and later suggested the war would end soon, insisting Tehran must never obtain a nuclear weapon.
Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday following reports that Vice President JD Vance had proposed renewed talks. Iranian sources said a meeting could take place within a week in Doha or Istanbul.
Pakistan’s military also expressed cautious optimism about its mediation efforts.
Yet reports that U.S. military officials briefed Trump on options for additional strikes, potentially after Tuesday’s midterm elections, highlighted the risk of renewed fighting. An Iranian official warned Tehran had prepared a broad response to any new attack.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the conflict had added more than €100 billion ($112 billion) to Europe’s energy costs and urged a negotiated settlement.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi responded with a warning of severe retaliation against countries attacking Iran, keeping the possibility of further disruption to energy shipments in focus.

title: Bitcoin holds above $77,000 as Binance hack recovery takes shape
full_text:
Investing.com -- Bitcoin traded slightly above $77,000 on Saturday as investors assessed fresh developments in the record $6.3 billion Binance hack, with Wall Street analysts suggesting the cryptocurrency’s recent selloff may have created buying opportunities.
The world’s largest cryptocurrency was trading down 1.71% at $77,175.4 as of 01:34 ET (05:34 GMT) after the security breach rattled digital asset markets late Thursday, triggering sharp declines in cryptocurrency-linked stocks.
Attention has shifted from the initial theft to the attackers’ efforts to move stolen funds and the industry’s ability to contain the damage.
Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis identified previously unseen laundering patterns involving thousands of transactions, suggesting hackers deployed automated systems to conceal stolen assets.
Investigators linked the activity to Tradertraitor, a North Korean hacking group, after identifying connections between the stolen Binance assets and funds taken during September’s Bitget breach.
The attackers also converted $325 million in stablecoins into approximately $285 million in ether, apparently seeking to move funds beyond the reach of issuer-controlled freezes.
Binance, meanwhile, outlined plans to restore withdrawals in phases following security checks and said it had reserved more than $6.34 billion in company funds to cover losses.
The exchange also plans to publish proof-of-reserves data by Monday, November 2, providing investors with another measure of its financial position.
Despite the disruption, analysts at Cantor Fitzgerald, TD Cowen and Compass Point argued that the breach does not necessarily threaten Bitcoin’s underlying technology or the broader market’s recovery.
Cantor analyst Ramsey El-Assal viewed weakness in cryptocurrency-linked equities as a potential buying opportunity.
Compass Point identified the $75,000 to $77,000 range as an important support area for Bitcoin, warning that a sustained break below those levels could threaten its recent recovery.
Separately, Tether reported $1.5 billion in third-quarter operating profit, bringing its nine-month total to $4.5 billion.
The stablecoin issuer’s reserves reached $191.5 billion, exceeding liabilities by nearly $8 billion.
The figures provided another indication of the financial resources available within the stablecoin sector as issuers face renewed scrutiny over their ability to freeze stolen assets.
Legal experts cautioned that freezing tokens does not automatically establish ownership or guarantee their recovery, leaving the outcome of the Binance investigation uncertain.

title: Agentic AI excitement runs ahead of results
full_text:
Investing.com -- Investor enthusiasm for agentic artificial intelligence is growing faster than the technology’s ability to generate meaningful revenue and productivity gains, according to a report from BCA Research.
In an October 23 report, BCA Research chief technology and innovation strategist Matt Dyson warned that sustaining positive sentiment through 2027 would require stronger AI revenues or a breakthrough application, such as capable personal assistants.
The firm highlighted a persistent gap between AI adoption and measurable financial returns.
A 2025 MIT study suggested that 95% of corporate AI pilots failed to achieve deployment with positive returns within six months. A 2026 McKinsey survey found that just 6% of respondents attributed at least 5% of operating earnings to AI adoption.
BCA estimated that AI systems with human oversight could perform certain tasks at approximately 75% lower cost than U.S. employees.
Yet those savings often overlook what the firm calls the "AI validation tax," referring to the additional time employees spend checking AI-generated work.
The report also questioned whether surging AI token consumption accurately reflects productive usage.
More sophisticated reasoning models consume four to 15 times as many tokens, helping explain rapid demand growth without a corresponding increase in useful output.
Agentic AI has also raised concerns about traditional software companies.
The launch of Anthropic’s Claude Cowork plugins contributed to a 15% decline in the MSCI U.S. IT Services index in January, affecting companies including Salesforce, Intuit and Workday.
BCA described the market reaction as excessive, arguing that smaller businesses would likely continue favoring established software platforms.
The firm expects companies to need at least a year to restructure workflows around AI capabilities.
Dyson also warned that only 20% of freelance tasks completed by leading AI models currently meet reasonable client acceptance standards, highlighting the gap between technical performance and commercial usefulness.

title: Russia says Ukraine peace stance unchanged as Lavrov criticizes Zelenskiy
full_text:
Investing.com -- Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Friday that Moscow’s position on the Ukraine war remains unchanged, warning that President Volodymyr Zelenskiy’s continued support for strikes on Russian targets could complicate efforts to restart peace negotiations.
Speaking on the sidelines of a G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, Lavrov questioned Ukraine’s intentions ahead of potential trilateral negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine and the U.S.
He said Zelenskiy’s repeated statements about acquiring additional weapons to strike Russian targets were making preparations for fresh negotiations more difficult.
Both Moscow and Kyiv have expressed willingness to resume three-way discussions for the first time since early 2026.
Zelenskiy said this week that he hoped negotiators would meet in Abu Dhabi between November 6 and 10, adding that Ukraine wanted European representatives involved in discussions on ending the conflict.
Lavrov reiterated Moscow’s longstanding position that Ukraine must not pose a military threat to Russia’s security interests.
The Russian foreign minister also criticized Washington’s continued military assistance to Kyiv, arguing that fundamental disagreements between Moscow and the U.S. remained unresolved.
He pointed to ongoing sanctions against Russia and increased U.S. intelligence cooperation with Ukraine.
Lavrov specifically cited Friday’s U.S. State Department approval of a proposed sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine as evidence that Washington’s military support was continuing.
Separately, Lavrov criticized the U.S. decision to invite Poland to the G20 gathering, arguing that the move violated diplomatic practices requiring consensus among member countries.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said Washington had proposed making Poland a permanent G20 member, an initiative Warsaw was actively pursuing.
Lavrov dismissed Poland’s participation, arguing that existing NATO and European Union members already provided sufficient regional representation.
Sikorski also called for an immediate ceasefire in the Black Sea to permit safe grain shipments from both Ukraine and Russia.
The meeting’s proceedings showed the diplomatic disagreements, as foreign ministers skipped the traditional group photo after some participants objected to appearing alongside Lavrov.

title: What comes next for EU-China trade?
full_text:
Investing.com -- Trade tensions between the European Union and China could intensify in 2027 as Brussels considers additional measures to address its widening trade deficit with Beijing, although a full-scale trade war remains unlikely, according to Citi analysts.
In a research note, Citi said the recent EU-China agreement to restrict Chinese hybrid-vehicle exports could provide a foundation for broader negotiations, but warned that further trade restrictions remained possible.
The agreement comes as Europe’s trade deficit with China exceeds €1 billion per day, prompting European officials to consider stronger measures to rebalance bilateral trade.
China’s trade surplus with the EU reached $291.7 billion in 2025, an increase of 18.1% from the previous year and more than double the $113.8 billion recorded in 2019.
Chinese exports to the bloc rose 8.4% in 2025, while imports from Europe declined 0.4%, widening the imbalance.
The trend accelerated during the first nine months of 2026, with China’s trade surplus with the EU increasing 26% from a year earlier.
China’s share of total EU imports also climbed to 22.4% in 2025, even as Europe’s share of Chinese imports continued to decline.
Citi expects Brussels could introduce further trade measures targeting Chinese goods, potentially increasing friction between the two economies.
Beijing may respond by offering practical concessions, including commitments to increase imports, agreements covering specific industries and reductions in value-added tax export rebates.
The analysts believe the prospect of substantial economic damage on both sides should discourage an escalation comparable to the 2025 U.S.-China trade confrontation.
Still, prolonged uncertainty over trade policy could weigh on economic growth in 2027.
For China, the risks are particularly significant as policymakers face increasing pressure to maintain annual economic growth near 4%.
The bank expects trade-related uncertainty to remain a significant challenge for Chinese exports and the broader economy next year.

title: Is the market too bearish on aluminium?
full_text:
Investing.com -- Investor sentiment toward aluminium has turned excessively bearish despite resilient demand and historically low inventories, according to analysts who expect prices to rise to $3,625 per tonne in 2027.
The analysts said discussions with market participants pointed to unusually negative sentiment, but argued that aluminium’s underlying supply-demand fundamentals supported a more constructive outlook.
Their assessment followed Norsk Hydro’s (OSL) third-quarter results, which showed stronger year-on-year earnings but fell short of market expectations.
The Norwegian aluminium producer reported EBITDA of NOK 9.1 billion, up 52% from a year earlier and 2% sequentially, but 6% below consensus estimates.
Higher aluminium prices supported earnings, although rising costs and foreign exchange movements weighed on profitability.
Performance varied across divisions, with Bauxite and Alumina exceeding reduced expectations and Extrusions outperforming forecasts. Primary Metal, Markets and Energy delivered weaker results.
The analysts lowered their 2026 EBITDA forecast by 4% to NOK 34.9 billion and reduced their price target to NOK 92 from NOK 98, maintaining a Buy rating.
Hydro also lowered its capital expenditure guidance to NOK 12.5 billion from NOK 13.5 billion.
Operational disruptions remained a concern after a temporary natural gas supply interruption affected the Alunorte alumina refinery.
Production has returned to normal following alternative LNG arrangements, although elevated energy costs are expected to persist into the fourth quarter.
Meanwhile, Hydro has begun restarting its Slovalco smelter in Slovakia, targeting annual production capacity of 75,000 tonnes by February 2027.
The company’s downstream Extrusions business also showed signs of recovery following an extended downturn.
Improving recycling margins, better cost performance and stabilising market conditions supported the division’s third-quarter performance.
The analysts expect higher volumes and steadier margins ahead, reinforcing their view that aluminium market pessimism may be overstated.

title: OpenAI raises just $11bn of $30bn target as AI investor appetite cools - WSJ
full_text:
Investing.com -- OpenAI has secured approximately $11 billion in commitments for its latest funding round, falling well short of its initial $30 billion target as investor concerns over artificial intelligence spending intensify, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday.
The financing values the ChatGPT maker at $1.25 trillion, below the $1.4 trillion valuation it initially sought, according to the report.
OpenAI has struggled to attract sufficient interest from some major investors amid growing concerns about the financial sustainability of the AI industry’s rapid expansion.
The company has reportedly reduced its fundraising ambitions to as much as $20 billion and plans to approach family offices and wealthy individuals in the coming weeks to secure additional commitments.
The fundraising difficulties come as OpenAI prepares for a potential initial public offering as early as next year.
Investor sentiment toward AI companies has weakened following disappointing earnings from major technology companies, including Google, Amazon and Intel, which contributed to a broader selloff in technology stocks.
The setback also comes as OpenAI faces intensifying competition from Anthropic, whose Claude Code platform has attracted substantial demand from enterprise customers and software developers.
Anthropic more than doubled its quarterly revenue to $11.6 billion in the second quarter, compared with the first quarter, according to figures cited in the report.
OpenAI’s revenue increased approximately 18% over the same period to $6.7 billion.
Anthropic also recorded a small operating profit during the second quarter, contrasting with widening operating losses at OpenAI.
The competing AI developer has filed paperwork for a public listing expected next month, potentially putting additional pressure on OpenAI ahead of its own anticipated market debut.
OpenAI has recently regained some market share from Anthropic after reducing prices for its latest AI models, according to third-party data cited in the report.

title: Tech risk-reward turns favorable after rout, Deutsche Bank says
full_text:
Investing.com -- Deutsche Bank has upgraded global technology stocks to "overweight" after a sharp market selloff and a retreat in investor positioning improved the sector's risk-reward profile, arguing that much of the concern around AI demand is already reflected in valuations.
The bank's strategists, led by Parag Thatte and Chief Strategist Binky Chadha, said mega-cap growth and technology stocks had underperformed the rest of the S&P 500 by more than 16 percentage points over three weeks.
The technology group fell 11% during the period, while the remainder of the benchmark gained almost 6%, pushing relative performance to the bottom of its decade-long trend channel.
Deutsche Bank said investor positioning had also retreated from elevated levels to neutral, bringing exposure more closely in line with an anticipated earnings growth rate of around 10%. That compares with earnings growth of about 47% in the third quarter and consensus expectations of 36% by the end of next year.
The bank noted that previous rotations back into technology had delivered an average gain of 32%, outperforming the rest of the S&P 500 by 30 percentage points. The broader benchmark also gained an average 16% over the three months following those rotations.
Deutsche Bank pointed to continued strength in corporate earnings beyond technology.
Although technology and energy account for approximately three-quarters of expected third-quarter S&P 500 earnings growth of 31%, earnings growth excluding those sectors remains a robust 12%. The median S&P 500 company is expected to deliver growth of 14.4%, close to a two-decade high outside recessionary rebounds.
The bank acknowledged risks from potential technology regulation following the US midterm elections and further geopolitical escalation, but argued that equity and oil markets had already priced in substantial uncertainty. Oil prices were approximately 65% above its estimate of medium-term fair value.
Deutsche Bank said the recent correction had created a more attractive entry point, although further downside remained possible in the event of another major external shock.

title: Iran state media says U.S. attacked fishing boats near Qeshm Island
full_text:
Investing.com -- Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, citing an official in Hormozgan province, said on Saturday that the United States attacked two fishing boats near Qeshm Island, leaving two fishermen missing and one wounded.
There was no immediate U.S. confirmation of the reported attack.
The incident comes amid continued diplomatic efforts to end the eight-month conflict. Pakistan's military is "cautiously optimistic" about its mediation between Washington and Tehran, its spokesman Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry told Reuters in an exclusive interview published on Friday.
Chaudhry said Pakistan army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir's two visits to Tehran this month indicated some positive momentum, although he warned that there were still "powerful spoilers and detractors" who believed the conflict served their interests. Munir's latest visit on Monday also included Saudi and Turkish officials.
U.S. President Donald Trump separately said on Friday that he believed the war would end soon, telling Kansas City radio station KCMO that it was "going to get wrapped up soon". He added that Washington needed a guarantee that Iran would never possess a nuclear weapon, without providing details on how an agreement could be reached.
Trump has also said the United States would not strike Iran before the November 3 midterm elections.
The latest reported incident highlights the continued security risks in the region even as diplomatic efforts gather pace, with no confirmed breakthrough in negotiations.

title: Power bills and data centers cast rare spotlight on utilities in US midterms
full_text:
NEW YORK, Oct 31 (Reuters) - US electricity prices had flown under the radar in past national elections, but they have become a major political issue in this year’s midterms as Americans grow angry over rising utility bills and deals for power-hungry data centers.
Nationwide, according to Energy Information Administration data, electricity prices for homes have risen more than 10% since 2024 when President Donald Trump was elected along with Republican majorities in both houses of the US Congress. Higher electricity prices have outpaced the rise in costs for other goods and services.
Power bills have grown even faster in political battleground states of Ohio, Michigan and Pennsylvania, which are also hot spots for new data centers. In some cases, electricity bills have soared by triple the inflation rate.
Many politicians vying for top statehouse seats across the country this year have backed cracking down on utilities. Some have proposed freezing utility rate increases and slashing guaranteed returns, steps that could have sweeping consequences for the country’s utility industry.
"It could be the first election to feature utilities and electricity, specifically, as a prominent issue in the midterms," said Charles Hua, executive director of PowerLines, a nonprofit that advocates reforming utility policy to favor consumers. "Part of that is because people’s utility bills have gone up and up, and they don’t see any end in sight."
Utilities are heavily regulated. State regulators generally must approve utilities’ requests to spend on the grid and to recover those costs through rate increases. Regulators also set the return on equity utilities can earn on their grid investments.
This year, utilities are on track to match last year’s record high $31 billion in rate increase requests to regulators, a PowerLines survey showed. Last year’s spending was double the previous record.
The investor-owned companies are also expected to carry out a record of nearly $1.3 trillion in capital spending over the next five years, according to an analysis by S&P Global’s Regulatory Research Associates.
UTILITIES SPOTLIGHTED
Seats on nine state public utility commissions are up for election this year, nearly all the US states where voters elect their utility regulators. These include burgeoning data center hubs Arizona and Georgia.
Governors will be chosen in 36 US states this year, and governors appoint utility regulators in states where commissioners are not directly elected.
In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton has promised to lower energy bills if she is elected governor. Her campaign said she will also appoint a public utilities commission that was "not beholden to utility companies" and work with the state attorney general to crack down on "excessive rate hikes and predatory practices."
Ohio’s residential electricity bills have grown by more than 20% over the last two years, according to EIA data.
Acton has also said she supports a data center moratorium. Her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy said he would assure Ohioans living near data centers would not pay electricity bills at all.
BULLY PULPIT
Some governors who are up for reelection have used their political weight to pressure the power industry to keep prices down.
In April, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro announced that prominent utility, PECO Energy Company, had acceded to his demand that it withdraw its proposal with state regulators to increase rates. Shapiro, a Democrat running for reelection, said the move would reduce future utility bills by as much as $34 a month.
He followed up with a letter to more utility CEOs seeking changes in how utilities justify spending and returns on equity.
"The governors are using this crisis on energy affordability as an opportunity to take a deeper dive into the utility regulatory model and see if it makes any sense," said Jamie Van Nostrand, senior fellow at the Kleinman Center for Energy Policy at the University of Pennsylvania and former chair of the Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities.
Power bills tracked low inflation for roughly a decade, and were not an issue in most mainstream elections until last year, when Mikie Sherrill successfully ran for New Jersey governor on the promise of freezing utility bills. She did so the same day she took office.
In Virginia, home to the largest concentration of data centers in the world, Governor Abigail Spanberger took a similar approach, which industry analysts said could offer a playbook for those who win this year’s elections.
Utility advocates say reducing guaranteed returns and freezing rates will not make a meaningful difference in household bills but could lead to a long-term reduction of investments in the grid.
"The grid is America’s greatest machine, and it doesn’t operate on the political calendar,” said Drew Maloney, president of Edison Electric Institute, a trade organization for investor-owned electric utilities. “It requires consistent investment every year to deliver reliable energy to our customers."
Credit rating agency Fitch downgraded the North American utility sector to "deteriorating" from "neutral" in June, citing political pressure in the midterms to limit electricity bills and utility profits.
For an industry that plans in decades, it is hard to predict the result of short-term political moves aimed at saving money for households.
"I do think the real meat will come after the election," Hua said.

title: Coal supply is struggling to keep pace with demand
full_text:
Investing.com -- Global coal supply is struggling to keep pace with rising Asian demand as production constraints and higher natural gas prices tighten the market, potentially pushing thermal coal prices higher this winter, according to Bank of America (BofA) analysts.
Benchmark Australian Newcastle thermal coal prices have surged 40% this year to around $150 per metric ton, their highest level in two years, supported by stronger consumption and limited seaborne supplies.
BofA expects prices to remain supported through winter as elevated natural gas costs encourage power producers to switch to coal, particularly across Asia.
The Middle East conflict has tightened liquefied natural gas supplies, pushing Asian JKM prices above $30 per million British thermal units and European TTF prices beyond €90 per megawatt-hour this month.
At current gas prices, BofA estimates Newcastle coal could reach more than $350 per ton before losing its cost advantage over natural gas, suggesting considerable room for coal prices to rise.
South Korea has led recent demand growth, alongside emerging Asian economies including Vietnam and Pakistan, where higher energy costs have strengthened coal’s appeal.
Supply pressures are also mounting in China and India, the world’s largest coal consumers.
China’s stricter oversight of mine safety and excessive production has constrained domestic output growth as utilities prepare for winter.
In India, weaker-than-expected production and sustained power generation have depleted inventories, with power plant coal stocks falling more than 60% from their March peak.
BofA expects restocking in both countries to support import demand over the coming months.
Meanwhile, Indonesian coal exports have declined following government production cuts and drought-related disruptions to coal transportation.
Russian shipments remain restricted by financial and logistical challenges, with vessel attacks effectively halting exports from Azov and Black Sea ports.
Increased shipments from Australia, the U.S., South Africa, and Colombia have partly offset these shortfalls, but BofA warned that limited spare export capacity leaves global coal markets vulnerable to further supply disruptions.

title: Preschool case tests religious conservatives’ US Supreme Court win streak
full_text:
WASHINGTON, Oct 31 (Reuters) - A challenge at the US Supreme Court by Catholic groups to a Colorado law barring anti-LGBT discrimination at publicly funded preschools is testing whether conservative religious interests can extend their winning streak in major cases at the nation’s top judicial body.
The court, whose 6-3 conservative majority has taken a broad view of religious liberty, will hear arguments on Tuesday over a bid by the Archdiocese of Denver and other Catholic entities for an exemption from a Colorado preschool funding program’s nondiscrimination requirement. Republican President Donald Trump’s administration is backing the Catholic groups.
Officials in Democratic-governed Colorado have accused the Catholic preschools of seeking legal permission to discriminate against 4-year-olds and their families while receiving taxpayer dollars.
The case will give the court an opportunity to further expand the sweep of a provision of the US Constitution’s First Amendment called the Free Exercise Clause, which protects the right to practice religion without government interference.
It also represents the latest clash between religious rights and LGBT protections at the court, where conservative religious interests in recent years have prevailed in a series of such disputes.
CONSTITUTIONAL RELIGION PROVISIONS
"These cases reflect a very conservative court, following the conservative agenda on the religion clauses and LGBT issues," Erwin Chemerinsky, dean of the University of California, Berkeley Law School, said of the recent rulings.
The First Amendment religion provisions also include the Establishment Clause, which restricts the government from establishing or endorsing any particular religion, or promoting religion over nonreligion. This provision underpins the concept of separation of church and state.
Colorado children in 2023 became eligible under state law for 15 hours per week of state-funded preschool before entering kindergarten. Participating preschools may be public or private, secular or religious. But in each case, under the law, schools must give all children "equal opportunity" to enroll, regardless of the sexual orientation or gender identity of the students or parents.
The Archdiocese of Denver along with other Catholic entities and a Colorado family sued as the state’s universal preschool initiative was ramping up. They argued that the program’s anti-discrimination mandate burdened their religious exercise.
The archdiocese oversees 34 Catholic preschools, according to court papers. Its policy is to admit students only from families who support Catholic beliefs, including on same-sex relationships and gender identity.
The Catholic Church recognizes marriage as a union only between a man and a woman, not same-sex couples, and opposes transgender self-identification. The Catholic Church’s catechism, a compendium of its teachings, also states that "homosexual acts are intrinsically disordered" and that "under no circumstances can they be approved."
A Colorado-based federal judge in 2024 upheld the state program’s protections for LGBT people. The Denver-based 10th US Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed that ruling last year, prompting the current appeal to the Supreme Court.
GAY MARRIAGE DECISION
Citing the Supreme Court’s 2015 ruling that legalized gay marriage nationwide, lawyers for the Catholic preschools told the justices in a filing that the court in that decision promised "that religious groups would be protected when they dissent from secular orthodoxies about marriage and sexuality."
"The Free Exercise Clause simply cannot do that important work — which this court has described as ’at the heart of our pluralistic society’ — if it can be so easily evaded," they wrote.
The challengers are represented by the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, a conservative legal group whose website touts its "unparalleled, undefeated record" in 13 cases before the Supreme Court, 6 of which were unanimous decisions.
SCALIA RULING IN CONSERVATIVE CROSSHAIRS
Colorado has argued that its equal-opportunity requirements do not intrude on the Free Exercise Clause because they are neutral and apply generally to participating groups.
Colorado bases its argument on a 1990 Supreme Court precedent in a case called Employment Division v. Smith that upheld "generally applicable" laws even if they curb religious freedom. Despite being authored by the staunchly conservative late Justice Antonin Scalia, that ruling has long been in the crosshairs of conservative litigants.
The Supreme Court, in agreeing to hear the Colorado case, formally declined to consider overruling Smith. But a group of constitutional scholars who back Colorado cautioned the justices that embracing the broadest argument presented by the Catholic groups would gut the precedent.
Doing so, they argued in a filing, would usher in a "most-favored nation" rule for religion, meaning that exceptions granted for secular activities would make it difficult for states to deny comparable exceptions for religious activities.
"The original public meaning of the (Free Exercise) Clause is that it forbids laws targeting religion as such, not that it affirmatively requires religious exemptions from laws that the state permissibly enacts," the scholars wrote in their brief.
A core disagreement in the case is whether Colorado discriminated against the Catholic preschools by refusing to exempt them from the equal-opportunity requirement, while at the same time allowing preschools to prioritize the enrollment of low-income and disabled students.
The court’s thinking on this question may be guided by its recent decisions that expanded access by religious schools to public money in response to policies that, in the view of the justices, had unlawfully excluded religious institutions.
A SERIES OF MAJOR RULINGS
In 2022, the court ruled in favor of two Christian families in their challenge to a Maine program that provided state-funded tuition assistance that had excluded private religious schools. In 2020, it endorsed Montana tax credits that helped pay for students to attend private religious schools, ruling in favor of three mothers of Christian school students.
Those decisions followed the court’s 2017 ruling in favor of Trinity Lutheran Church of Columbia, Missouri, that declared that churches and other religious entities cannot be flatly denied public money based on their religious status — even in states whose constitutions explicitly ban such funding.
Advocacy groups backing Colorado, including the ACLU and Americans United for Separation of Church and State, told the justices in a filing that the state’s preschool funding program is neutral toward religion.
Siding with the Catholic groups, they argued, would force the government "to provide taxpayer dollars – and the state’s imprimatur – to beneficiaries whose conduct undercuts state policy goals, including equality goals."
In several recent cases the Supreme Court has sided with conservative religious litigants over competing LGBT interests.
The court in March rejected a Colorado law that barred psychotherapists from using "conversion" talk therapy intended to change an LGBT minor’s sexual orientation or gender identity, siding with a Christian licensed counselor in casting the ban as an intrusion on First Amendment free speech rights.
The court last year sided with Christian and Muslim parents in Maryland who sued to keep their elementary school children out of certain classes when storybooks with LGBT characters are read.
In another blow to LGBT rights, the court ruled in 2023 that the First Amendment right to free speech allows certain businesses to refuse to provide services for same-sex weddings. And in 2018, it sided with a Colorado baker who refused based on his Christian beliefs to have his shop make a wedding cake for a gay couple, based on the Free Exercise Clause.
The court’s liberal justices have raised the alarm in recent cases, arguing that the conservative majority is undermining church-state separation as envisioned in the Establishment Clause.
Dissenting in the 2022 case from Maine, liberal Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote, "Today, the court leads us to a place where separation of church and state becomes a constitutional violation."

title: BOJ speeds up ETF sales, potentially boosting funding for Takaichi’s plans
full_text:
Investing.com -- The Bank of Japan’s decision to accelerate sales of its exchange-traded fund holdings could generate additional government revenue, potentially helping Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi finance her ambitious spending plans.
The central bank announced Friday that it would increase annual ETF sales to ¥860 billion ($5.5 billion) on a book-value basis starting in January, compared with the current ¥330 billion.
The faster pace would reduce the estimated time required to unwind its ETF holdings to approximately 43 years from 112 years.
Under Japanese law, the BOJ must transfer surplus earnings to the government after accounting for dividends and other expenses.
Accelerating ETF sales could increase realized capital gains and boost these payments, providing additional non-tax revenue for the government.
Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said Friday that higher ETF sales should increase the central bank’s surplus earnings and government remittances.
She added that officials would assess how to allocate the additional funds during the upcoming budget process.
Taro Kimura, a senior economist at Bloomberg Economics, estimated that the accelerated sales could generate approximately ¥800 billion in additional annual revenue for the BOJ.
The potential revenue increase comes as Takaichi prepares to finance several major policy commitments, including a two-year reduction in food consumption taxes, a 14-year investment programme and increased defense spending.
Japan’s government is also considering establishing a dedicated economic security account to support longer-term strategic investments.
Kazumasa Ishii, a strategist at UBS SuMi TRUST Wealth Management, said additional BOJ payments would be better suited to financing multi-year programmes than offsetting temporary revenue losses from tax reductions.
The accelerated ETF disposal programme could provide another source of government funding as Japan balances fiscal expansion with the central bank’s gradual withdrawal from unconventional monetary policies.

title: Mizuho favors these U.S. restaurant stocks ahead of earnings
full_text:
Investing.com -- Mizuho Securities expects Dutch Bros, BJ's Restaurants and Texas Roadhouse to deliver stronger sales growth than analysts anticipate as menu innovation, value-focused promotions and improving customer traffic support restaurant operators heading into the third-quarter earnings season.
The brokerage identified the three companies as its top picks ahead of a busy week of restaurant earnings, citing opportunities for stronger comparable-store sales and improved profit growth. However, it flagged continued uncertainty around consumer spending, inconsistent sales trends and cost pressures across the sector.
Dutch Bros remains Mizuho's top pick, with analysts expecting comparable-store sales growth of 6.3% in the third quarter, above the 6.0% consensus estimate. The coffee chain could benefit from food sales, increased mobile ordering and loyalty engagement, menu innovation and marketing investment. Mizuho expects stronger sales to support upward revisions to earnings estimates through 2027, although it lowered its price target to $65 from $80, citing lower valuations across peer companies.
The forecasts highlight a widening divide among restaurant operators as investors assess which chains can sustain traffic growth and protect margins in a challenging consumer environment. Mizuho favors companies with clearer sales-growth drivers, while remaining cautious about businesses facing inconsistent demand, turnaround risks or limited visibility into longer-term performance.
The earnings reports are scheduled for November 4 and 5. Dutch Bros, Cava Group, Dine Brands Global and McDonald's are due to report on November 4, while BJ's Restaurants, Shake Shack, Papa John's and Texas Roadhouse are scheduled to report on November 5.
BJ's Restaurants is also expected to outperform expectations, with Mizuho forecasting comparable-store sales growth of 5.5%, compared with the 4.8% consensus estimate. Seasonal Pizookies, its $13.99 Pizookie Meal Deal, weekday lunch promotions and menu improvements are expected to support customer traffic. The brokerage also anticipates better profit flow-through from sales growth than in the previous quarter and expects the momentum to continue into 2027. It maintained an Outperform rating and a $76 price target.
Texas Roadhouse could see its sales growth recover after a mid-October trough, according to Mizuho's checks. The brokerage attributed a 2%-3% slowdown in September comparable-store sales to backlash following allegations circulated on social media in August. It expects a gradual recovery through the fourth quarter as the company addresses the controversy through marketing and communications.
Mizuho maintained its third-quarter comparable-store sales growth estimate of 5.0% for Texas Roadhouse but forecast fourth-quarter growth of 3.5%, below the 4.5% consensus estimate. It expects the impact of the controversy to fade by year-end and projects comparable-store sales growth of 5.4% in 2027, above the 4.8% consensus. The brokerage raised its price target to $220 from $190, citing improving visibility into sales recovery and the potential for lower beef costs to support margins.
The outlook is more cautious for McDonald's, where persistent pressure on lower-income consumers, elevated gasoline prices and difficult comparisons could weigh on U.S. sales. Mizuho expects U.S. comparable-store sales to decline 0.5% in the third quarter and lowered its fourth-quarter estimate to flat growth from 1.0%. It cut its price target to $260 from $290 and maintained a Neutral rating.
Cava Group faces uncertainty over the durability of its sales growth beyond 2026, despite an expected recovery following the impact of a Cyclospora outbreak on customer traffic. Mizuho expects third-quarter comparable-store sales growth of 3.5%, slightly above the 3.4% consensus estimate, but lowered its price target to $56 from $70, citing lower valuations among growth-oriented restaurant peers.
Papa John's outlook remains pressured by weak comparable-store sales, restructuring costs and uncertainty surrounding its turnaround. Mizuho expects North American franchised comparable-store sales to fall 8.0% in the third quarter, compared with the 7.7% decline expected by analysts. It lowered its price target to $20 from $26 and maintained a Neutral rating.
Shake Shack, meanwhile, is expected to benefit from menu innovation and promotional activity, particularly in the fourth quarter. Mizuho forecasts third-quarter comparable-store sales growth of 1.2%, below the 1.5% consensus estimate, but expects fourth-quarter growth of 2.0%, above the 1.4% consensus. It maintained an Outperform rating while lowering its price target to $80 from $90.

title: Samsung hosts OpenAI’s Altman for talks on AI chips and infrastructure
full_text:
Investing.com -- OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman met with senior Samsung Group executives in South Korea on Saturday to strengthen cooperation on memory chips and artificial intelligence infrastructure as global semiconductor shortages intensify.
Samsung hosted Altman and approximately 50 executives from its electronics, financial services and biotechnology businesses in Yongin, south of Seoul, according to a company statement.
The discussions examined how artificial intelligence could transform industries, corporate decision-making and business opportunities over the next decade.
The meeting comes as surging demand for AI computing infrastructure places increasing pressure on global memory chip supplies, driving prices higher and creating challenges for electronics manufacturers.
Major technology companies are accelerating investments in AI data centers, with the five largest participants in the infrastructure expansion planning more than $3 trillion in spending over the coming years.
Memory chips account for approximately one-third of data center spending, making access to sufficient supplies increasingly important for companies developing large-scale AI systems.
Saturday’s discussions build on an existing partnership between OpenAI and Samsung to supply memory chips for the ChatGPT maker’s Stargate infrastructure project.
The companies have also agreed to cooperate on AI data center development, including plans involving floating offshore facilities.
South Korea has become an increasingly important destination for U.S. technology executives seeking closer relationships with leading semiconductor manufacturers.
NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang and Advanced Micro Devices Inc (NASDAQ:AMD) CEO Lisa Su have each visited the country twice since last year as their companies work to strengthen supply chains.
Industry executives have warned that semiconductor manufacturing capacity is struggling to keep pace with accelerating demand from AI developers and data center operators.
Samsung is also expanding AI adoption across its own operations, including research, manufacturing, marketing, and corporate management.
The company’s involvement in both semiconductor production and AI infrastructure development positions it as a major supplier to technology companies investing heavily in next-generation computing systems.

title: US campaign for control of Congress enters final weekend
full_text:
WASHINGTON/ANCHORAGE, Oct 31 (Reuters) - As the campaign for control of the US Congress reached its final weekend, the Trump administration stepped up its legal intervention in the Alaska Senate race while the number of Americans casting early ballots neared 50 million, a record for a midterm election.
The Department of Justice accelerated its criminal investigation in Alaska on Friday, following reports that aides to a Democratic Senate candidate recruited a retired schoolteacher from a remote fishing village to get on the ballot because he has the same name as the Republican incumbent.
The DOJ, acting on a civil lawsuit that President Donald Trump said he instigated, also filed further motions in an attempt to block the state of Alaska from certifying the Senate results if the Republican incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan, loses a close race on a ballot that includes the nonpartisan candidate Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.
The closely contested race in Alaska is seen as crucial for the Democrats if they hope to take control of the Senate from Trump’s Republicans in Tuesday’s vote.
PROSECUTOR ALLEGES ’SHAM CANDIDATE’ IN KEY ALASKA RACE
It is one of 35 races in the 100-member Senate that will set the tone for Trump’s final two years in office. Also up for grabs are all 435 seats in the US House of Representatives.
Early voter participation this cycle has set a record. More than 49 million Americans have already cast ballots, either in person or by mail, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, up from nearly 46 million who voted before Election Day in the last midterms, in 2022.
A Democratic victory in one or both chambers could result in congressional investigations of the Trump administration, which for two years has enjoyed largely compliant Republican majorities.
Trump has been on a campaign blitz in multiple states over the past month but is not scheduled to travel on Saturday, when there will be a mash-up of American traditions: politics, Halloween and college football across the country. Trump returns to the campaign trail on Sunday in Kansas and Iowa.
The DOJ’s top prosecutor in Alaska, US Attorney Michael Heyman, said at a Friday press conference that a recent New York Times article about the supposed recruitment effort had driven a "surge" of FBI resources, adding that he had assigned several prosecutors to the case and that investigative steps were taking place "intensely and swiftly."
The Times reported on Wednesday that aides to Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola recruited Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. to run. Heyman labeled him a "sham candidate" but declined to say what crime may have been committed.
The department had already filed its civil action but, Heyman said, "when the New York Times article hit, that’s additional information that accelerated what we’ve been doing."
Peltola has denied knowing about any effort to recruit the second Sullivan. The retired teacher has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.
ADMINISTRATION GETS INVOLVED IN RACES NATIONWIDE
The Trump administration has also sued California to try to prevent the counting of ballots cast by more than 20,000 registered voters who the administration alleged could be noncitizens. It has also sued roughly 30 states and the District of Columbia, seeking unredacted voter rolls, part of a pattern that has alarmed election officials.
A federal judge on Friday ordered the DOJ to stop threatening to prosecute California election officials who do not comply with the Trump administration’s directives regarding alleged voting by noncitizens.
Sean Morales-Doyle, director of the voting rights and elections program at the Brennan Center for Justice, said the administration’s actions parallel the tactics undertaken by election deniers in the 2020 presidential election. While the administration is unlikely to win in court, he said, the efforts could create a political atmosphere that leads to official misconduct.
“It’s about creating uncertainty, sowing fear, distrust, chaos, hoping that you create the political circumstances in which maybe the lieutenant governor of Alaska does feel pressure to do something that they’re not supposed to do. Maybe the governor does start to question things, too,” Morales-Doyle said.
Even so, a bipartisan majority of US voters trust the overall electoral process, with 76% saying they are confident their ballots will be counted accurately, according to a September 30 to October 5 Reuters/Ipsos poll. Some 15% were not confident and the rest were not sure or did not answer the question. Confidence was about equally high among Republicans and Democrats.

title: UK PM Burnham says he is ’open’ to formal apology for slavery, but rules out reparations
full_text:
LONDON, Oct 31 (Reuters) - British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he is open to calls for a formal apology for Britain’s historical role in slavery, before attending next week’s Commonwealth summit at which he is likely to face demands for financial reparations.
Writing in the Guardian newspaper, Burnham said Britain was "offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade", in which at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery.
"Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them," he added.
But Burnham rejected calls for financial reparations, writing: "I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part."
From the 15th to the 19th century, millions of Africans were sold into slavery by European traders, with Britain transporting an estimated 3.2 million people across the Atlantic, according to the Transatlantic Slave Trade Database.
Ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda next week, King Charles, who is touring the Caribbean, said it was "only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past".
Caribbean leaders are expected to press demands for reparations, which they have often framed in terms of debt relief, development finance, education, healthcare and climate resilience.
Burnham also wrote in the Guardian that he wanted to "launch a new drive on debt", including by helping more vulnerable countries "repay over a longer time period and with better rates".
Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne welcomed Burnham’s comments and proposals for practical assistance, though he added in a Facebook post: "The Caribbean’s longstanding position on reparatory justice remains unchanged."

title: Rubio to host meeting of Indo-Pacific Quad, wrap up G20 gathering
full_text:
WASHINGTON, Oct 31 (Reuters) - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will host a meeting with the foreign ministers of Australia, India and Japan on Saturday, their third meeting this year, as plans take shape for a summit of the leaders of the four countries in Manila next month.
The leaders’ summit, slated to occur during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) conference in the Philippine capital November 15-18, will be the first since 2024, and the first for US President Donald Trump.
The first formal leaders’ summits of the four countries known as the Quad did not begin until President Joe Biden took office in 2021. Trump was scheduled to attend a Quad summit in India in late 2025, but canceled the visit due to trade frictions and tariff disputes with New Delhi.
After the Quad ministers’ meeting, Rubio will wrap up a two-day meeting of the Group of 20 major economies being held in Atlanta, after which he has invited the ministers to watch a college football game, according to the State Department schedule.
Rubio’s elder son, Anthony, is a running back for the University of Florida, which will be squaring off against the higher-ranked University of Georgia team.

title: ICE raids in a California toss-up district spark accusations of voter intimidation
full_text:
By Kristina Cooke and Marisa Taylor
BAKERSFIELD, California, Oct 31 (Reuters) - Federal immigration agents have fanned out across California’s Central Valley in recent weeks, stirring fear in Latino communities and allegations of voter intimidation in a toss-up race that could help decide control of the US House of Representatives.
The planned surge in California was announced to agents in early October, an internal email seen by Reuters shows. And it was directed by the White House, according to a US official, speaking on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
Unlike past operations in big cities like Minneapolis and Chicago that put hundreds of armed, masked agents on the streets, the surge here has been characterized by small groups of officers moving from town to town in the largely agricultural region. The United Farm Workers union said it knew of hundreds of California farmworkers detained in recent weeks.
In Bakersfield, immigration arrests jumped from one a day for much of the year to nearly 10 per day in mid-October, according to preliminary Department of Homeland Security data. In nearby Wasco, home to just 26,000 people, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested at least seven people in the span of a few days, the data showed.
The arrests have caused widespread alarm in the Latino-majority areas - and could have implications for Tuesday’s midterm elections, in which Republicans will be fighting to retain control of the House and Senate.
In California’s 22nd congressional district, which includes Bakersfield and is 73% Latino, polls have shown progressive Democrat Randy Villegas with a slight edge over six-term Republican incumbent David Valadao.
Villegas told reporters last week that the arrests were a “very clear attempt to try and intimidate our communities before this election."
Valadao said in a statement that he understood "the fear and uncertainty immigration enforcement has created for families throughout our communities," urging the Trump administration to "prioritize the removal of individuals who pose a threat to public safety."
The DHS, ICE’s parent agency, declined to comment on the California operations, citing concerns for officer safety, and did not respond to the allegations of voter intimidation.
“By all metrics, this should be a very close district,” said Thad Kousser, co-director of UC San Diego’s Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections. “Anything that drives voters to or away from the polls could matter.”
President Donald Trump made historic inroads with Hispanic voters in the 2024 election, but polls show public opinion has turned sharply against his immigration sweeps and economic policies.
Just 24% of Hispanic Americans approve of Trump’s performance, the lowest share in either of his presidential terms, a Reuters/Ipsos survey found last month.
In a statement, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said that Trump’s agenda had made Hispanic Americans “more prosperous and safer” and referred questions on ICE operations in California to DHS.
CLIMATE OF FEAR
Across the Central Valley, ICE has made arrests outside homes and at busy intersections, in strip mall parking lots, gas stations and near schools, according to lawyers, immigration advocates, videos and court records.
"Agents were given the green light to be out and make as many arrests as possible,” the US official said. Officers are also auditing records at local businesses and using employee information to arrest workers at their homes or on their daily commute, the official added.
Maribel Ramirez, a local farmworker, said the arrests have had a chilling effect on political activity in the area. She said that some young Hispanics with US citizenship have told her they are scared to vote, fearing it could expose the addresses of family members without legal status.
Even though voter information is meant to be private, some of “those who can vote won’t do so because their parents are immigrants,” she said.
Ramirez is urging every US citizen she knows to cast a ballot, “but not for anyone in red,” referring to Republicans.
Immigration activists in the area who have been sharing alerts about ICE sightings on social media are also, in some cases, sharing details about the midterm elections.
There are fewer people on the streets in Bakersfield, according to Ana Valencia, who owns a barber shop in town. Some local businesses are offering free delivery to those afraid to leave their homes.
Valencia says she voted early “because I don’t want ICE here, or anywhere really.”
Villegas has made the arrests a campaign issue, criticizing his opponent for voting to triple ICE’s budget and failing “to stand up for immigrant communities.”
Valadao has said ICE is targeting criminals in the community. In an interview with the Sacramento Bee published this week, he said the agency had gone too far in some cases but declined to give examples.
Jason Giannelli, 41, a fourth-generation farmer in Kern County who supports Valadao, said the Republican was “middle of the road” on immigration and “understands that probably ICE is going after the worst of the worst."
FARMWORKERS TARGETED
UFW national Vice President Elizabeth Strater told Reuters that the vast majority of farmworkers detained in recent weeks had no criminal records and some had legal work authorization.
A brother and sister from Mexico were unloading their shopping in a small town in Kern County in late October when immigration agents arrested them, a relative told Reuters, speaking on the condition of anonymity.
It was their day off from work in the fields nearby.
The agents were looking for someone else and did not know whom they had picked up until the handcuffs were on, according to a petition filed by the farmworkers’ lawyers in federal court contesting their detention as unlawful.
The sister arrived in the US as an unaccompanied minor more than a decade ago, according to the petition. The brother arrived as a toddler. Neither has criminal records, the petition says.
DHS said it did not have enough information to comment on the case.
On the day of the arrest, the woman’s 3-year old daughter was at daycare and her 11-year-old son was on a school camping trip. The children’s father had died suddenly this year, leaving their mother as the sole caregiver.
The 11-year-old returned home excited to see his mother, the relative said. When he heard she had been arrested, he broke down in tears and cried out for her.
The 3-year-old perks up whenever the phone rings, the relative said, asking if her mother is on the line.

title: France braces for fresh unrest, government vows tough response
full_text:
By Dominique Vidalon and Noemie Olive
PARIS, Oct 31 (Reuters) - France deployed a 70,000-strong police presence to contain a widely expected bout of fresh unrest on Saturday in the latest nationwide protests driven by anger over living costs, public services and President Emmanuel Macron’s government.
The demonstrations, which fall on Halloween, come two weeks after riots and looting caught security forces off guard, leaving damaged shops, public buildings and businesses in cities across France. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has vowed not to let a repeat happen.
"Everyone is on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble," Nunez told a news conference earlier this week as he set out details of security arrangements for a day he described as carrying "a very high risk" of unrest.
France’s top administrative court confirmed on Saturday a march between the emblematic Paris squares of Republique and Bastille will be banned, rejecting a challenge by unions. Demonstrations will instead have to be held on boulevards on the eastern fringe of the city, away from the main shopping areas in central Paris.
Authorities are also alert to the possibility that rioters could use Halloween masks to conceal their identities. Nunez noted that laws already allow police to ban face coverings when public order is at risk.
Some 150 gatherings were planned across France, the interior ministry said.
The US Embassy advised travellers to avoid areas where demonstrations or large gatherings are planned.
The protests gathered pace in late September as Macron’s minority government launched 2027 budget talks. Facing public debt approaching 120% of economic output and rising borrowing costs, the government is under pressure to rein in spending, narrowing its room for manoeuvre.
Students angry at the dilapidated state of many schools, crowded classes and a university admissions system widely seen as unfair, have been joined by trade unions and a re-emergent "Yellow Vest" movement demanding action on the cost of living.
PROTESTS SPREAD ACROSS EUROPE
The protests have inspired youth-led protests across Europe, with demonstrations planned in more than 30 German cities on Saturday.
The French government’s promises to reform education and ease fuel costs have failed to calm discontent.
"When I was little, I was told young people were the future," said Aaron Berthier de Grandry, a 15-year-old high school student in the Paris suburb of Nogent-sur-Marne who plans to join his third consecutive weekend of protests.
"Well, if we, as the future of France, lack resources, that means France will end up collapsing."
The unrest has handed a political boost to far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who leads opinion polls ahead of April’s presidential election, while potential centrist successors to Macron remain divided.
The troubles are the latest blow to an economy which, data on Friday showed, was already shrinking in the third quarter.
The Chamber of Commerce estimates losses to retailers exceed €1 billion ($1.1 billion). Other estimates put the total at double that when including uninsured damage and lost revenue.
Along Paris’ main shopping boulevards, early Christmas lights glow around boarded-up windows and security grilles. Among the shops targeted in previous unrest were outlets belonging to luxury brands including Hermes, Louis Vuitton and Burberry.
The government is pushing ahead with a controversial law making rioters liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage caused either by themselves or by groups they are deemed to be part of. Rights groups and some lawyers say the measure risks undermining the right to peaceful protest.

title: Citi explains what ’hawk’ and ’dove’ really mean as ECB faces leadership change
full_text:
Investing.com -- Citi has offered a fresh interpretation of what makes a central banker a hawk or a dove, arguing that the distinction is not simply about willingness to raise or cut interest rates, but reflects fundamentally different views on how inflation develops.
The distinction could become increasingly important for the European Central Bank as markets assess a possible early departure by its president and the prospect of several senior leadership changes in 2027.
Citi believes an early announcement of the president's departure could be imminent, potentially allowing governments to coordinate appointments to three key positions on the ECB's Executive Board.
Doves generally view inflation as the result of supply and demand imbalances. They distinguish between demand-driven or persistent supply shocks, which warrant a stronger monetary policy response, and temporary external shocks, such as an energy price spike, which they believe should be approached with greater patience.
Hawks, by contrast, place greater emphasis on inflation expectations. They believe that even temporary price increases can influence expectations and feed into future inflation, making a quicker policy response necessary to prevent expectations from becoming unanchored.
Citi said the difference also affects how policymakers view the risks of making a policy mistake. Doves are generally more concerned about inflation falling too low, given the difficulty of reviving demand once rates approach the lower bound. Hawks are more concerned about inflation overshooting its target, arguing that upward price pressures can become entrenched more quickly than deflationary forces.
The distinction is relevant to the ECB's recent communication, which Citi believes has shifted towards underlying inflation dynamics and monetary policy transmission, rather than near-term inflation projections alone.
Citi expects the ECB to leave rates unchanged at its October 29 meeting, followed by a 25-basis-point increase in December and potentially another in March 2027.
The bank expects the next ECB president, potentially Pablo Hernández de Cos or Klaas Knot, to have a significant influence on how the central bank weighs these competing considerations.

title: Bank of England weighs raising cap on high-risk mortgages to five times income: FT
full_text:
Investing.com -- The Bank of England is considering easing a key restriction on higher-risk mortgage lending, potentially giving lenders more scope to offer larger loans as policymakers face pressure to improve access to home ownership.
The central bank’s Financial Policy Committee is examining whether to raise the threshold for high loan-to-income (LTI) mortgages to five times household income, from 4.5 times currently, the Financial Times reported on Saturday.

The Bank of England’s Prudential Regulation Authority and Financial Conduct Authority implemented changes to the framework on October 28, removing the individual 15% cap for lenders while retaining the aggregate market-wide limit.
The latest Financial Policy Committee record showed high-LTI lending had reached 14.1% in the current quarter, with the four-quarter rolling average at 12%.
Raising the threshold to five times income could free up additional lending capacity equivalent to 7% of annual new residential mortgage lending, according to UK Finance estimates cited by the FT. High-LTI mortgages taken out by first-time buyers rose 66% in 2025, the newspaper reported.
The Bank of England told the FT that it regularly reviews its housing-related policy tools in light of the Financial Policy Committee’s objectives.
The review comes as the UK housing market shows signs of losing momentum. Nationwide data published Friday showed annual house price growth slowed to 0.5% in October from 0.8% in September, while prices were unchanged month on month.
